newsitem.title: POLAND: Polish TV suspends boss after violence allegations.
newsitem.headline: Polish TV suspends boss after violence allegations.

text.p: Poland's public television suspended its acting head of administration on Tuesday after press allegations that he once led a squad of violent communist activists who raided dissident intellectuals' homes.
"The management feels (Jerzy) Folcik will now be able, as a private person, to defend himself against press arguments," spokeswoman Joanna Bancerowska told PAP news agency.
Folcik told Reuters that the press charges were distorted and false, but that he did not plan to sue newspapers.

The daily Gazeta Wyborcza alleged at the weekend that Folcik had been a leading figure in a squad, cooperating with security police, which disrupted so-called "Flying University" lectures held in homes in the late 1970s by dissident intellectuals.
The most notorious event was in March 1979 at the home of dissident Jacek Kuron, now an opposition leader, when raiders attacked his wife and concussed his son and another guest.
"I see them tormenting my son, horribly and methodically. Several holding him and one beating," wrote Kuron in an account cited by Rzeczpospolita daily.
"In large measure they (press reports) are false, distorted, biased and the main theses are not true," Folcik said by telephone, saying he was being made a scapegoat for some ulterior reasons.
"But it is true that as a student I took part, I went to lectures, but I had nothing to do with any attacks," he said.
Folcik said he had been outside Kuron's building.

"I'm not saying there was no operations, there were, but... didn't see it as it took place on the stairs, and I was standing in front of the building...No one can accuse me of having hit or beaten anyone," he said.
"Only later, when I realised what was happening, I went in and -- this is why I am accused of being a leader -- I called on everyone to leave as fast as possible," Folcik said.

The allegations against Folcik have fuelled opposition charges that Poland's ruling communists, now social democrats, are packing the pre-1989 system's past supporters into the influential television and other key areas of public life.
Folcik got his senior job heading TV administrative offices last month with the support of a board member linked to the ruling Democratic Left Alliance (SLD), who quit last week.
SLD chiefs, while not disowning their past, say those guilty of communist-era abuses should be brought to book.
But opposition parties charge that the ex-communists are not pursuing those guilty of repression in the 1970s and 1980s.
Controversy has been fierce over the television, where supporters of the leftist coalition, which won power in 1993 polls, earlier this year gained control of management.
Public television is the main source of news for Poles and Washington officials this year voiced concern over what the TV management changes meant for Poland's young democracy.
Former U.S. president Jimmy Carter, now co-chairing a Commission on Radio and Television Policy, also wrote to Poland's President Aleksander Kwasniewski on this issue.
Kwasniewski, an ex-communist, replied to Carter on Friday that such concerns were unfounded as Polish law guaranteed freedom of the media.
